docs.title: Async kernel
docs.text: Async kernel is a Python Jupyter kernel that runs in an anyio event loop.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Execute requests
    • do not block shell messaging
    • are queued by default
    • can run concurrently (insert ##task or ##thread as the first line in a code cell)
    • use Context Variables to associate input and output with the originating cell
  • Launching custom kernels is supported
  • asyncio backed by default, trio backend configurable
  • wait_readable enables asychronous polling of zmq sockets (tornado-less)
  • Kernel debugging supported
  • Kernel requests run in a customised IPython shell supporting:
    • IPython
    • magic
    • code completion
    • widgets
    • matplotlib

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install async-kernel

To add a kernel spec for trio. 

pip install trio
async-kernel add async-trio

docs.title: Origin
docs.text: Async-kernel started as fork of IPyKernel commit #8322a7684b004ee95f07b2f86f61e28146a5996d.

docs.title: Caller
docs.text:
A class to enable calling functions and coroutines between anyio event loops.

The Caller class provides a mechanism to execute functions and coroutines in a dedicated thread, leveraging AnyIO for asynchronous task management. It supports scheduling calls with delays, executing them immediately, and running them without a context. It also provides a means to manage a pool of threads for general purpose offloading of tasks.

The class maintains a registry of instances, associating each with a specific thread. It uses a task group to manage the execution of scheduled tasks and provides methods to start, stop, and query the status of the caller.

Methods:

  • all_callers –

    Get a list of the callers.

  • as_completed –

    An iterator to get Futures as they complete.

  • call_later –

    Schedule func to be called in this instances event loop using the current contextvars context.

  • call_no_context –

    Call func in the thread event loop.

  • call_soon –

    Schedule func to be called in this instances event loop using the current contextvars context.

  • get_instance –

    Gets an instance of the Caller by name.

  • start_new –

    Start a new thread with a new Caller open in the context of anyio event loop.

  • stop –

    Stop the caller cancelling all pending tasks and close the thread.

  • stop_all –

    Stop all instances.

  • to_thread –

    Call func in a separate thread.

  • to_thread_by_name –

    Call the function in the Caller's thread.

Future(thread: Thread | None = None)

A class representing a future result modelled on the asyncio class Future .

This class provides an anyio compatible Future primative. It is designed to work with the Caller to enable thread-safe, event loop function calls.

    Return the exception that was set on this Future.

docs.title: Caller
docs.text:
To get the caller for the main thread.

Ensure you're running an async kernel.

In [ ]: Copied! 
from async_kernel import Caller

main_caller = Caller.get_instance()
main_caller
from async_kernel import Caller main_caller = Caller.get_instance() main_caller In [ ]: Copied! 
import random
import time

import ipywidgets as ipw

from async_kernel import Caller

outputs = {}


def my_func(n):
    caller = Caller()
    if not (out := outputs.get(caller)):
        outputs[caller] = out = ipw.HTML(description=str(caller))
        out.style.description_width = "220px"
        display(out)
    sleep_time = random.random() / 4
    out.value = f"{n=:04d} sleeping {sleep_time * 1000:03.0f} ms"
    time.sleep(sleep_time)
    return n


async def run_forever():
    n = 0
    while True:
        n += 1
        yield Caller.to_thread(my_func, n)


async for fut in Caller.as_completed(run_forever()):
    result = await fut
    print(f"Finished: {result}", end="\r")
import random import time import ipywidgets as ipw from async_kernel import Caller outputs = {} def my_func(n): caller = Caller() if not (out := outputs.get(caller)): outputs[caller] = out = ipw.HTML(description=str(caller)) out.style.description_width = "220px" display(out) sleep_time = random.random() / 4 out.value = f"{n=:04d} sleeping {sleep_time * 1000:03.0f} ms" time.sleep(sleep_time) return n async def run_forever(): n = 0 while True: n += 1 yield Caller.to_thread(my_func, n) async for fut in Caller.as_completed(run_forever()): result = await fut print(f"Finished: {result}", end="\r")

docs.title: Caller¶
docs.text:
Caller is a class that makes it easy to call code in different threads/tasks. One caller instance is created per thread, and each of those instances can be retrieved by name using the Caller.get_instance class method or in the thread in which it is running simply by Caller().

Caller is used by the kernel internally for running code, but can also be used directly by the user. Each caller starts its own iopub zmq socket.

docs.title: Threads¶
docs.text:
The caller manages a pool of worker threads (not related to anyio worker threads) or you can specify the name of a new thread which you can manage yourself. Each thread has its own anyio event loop in which the code will be called.

Most methods that perform execution return an async_kernel.Future.

docs.title: Usage by the kernel¶
docs.text:
The Kernel runs two threads; one each for the shell and control. The thread names are 'MainThread' and 'ControlThread' respectively. You can easily get the main thread caller by using the classmethod Caller.get_instance().

Kernel uses one of Caller().call_soon Caller.to_thread depending on the header directive

docs.title: Caller of the current thread¶
docs.text: To get the caller for the current thread use Caller(). It will raise a Runtime error if the thread doesn't have a running instance.

docs.title: Code Styling
docs.text:
ipykernel has adopted automatic code formatting so you shouldn't need to worry too much about your code style. As long as your code is valid, the pre-commit hook should take care of how it should look. To install pre-commit, run the following::

pip install pre-commit
pre-commit install

You can invoke the pre-commit hook by hand at any time with::

pre-commit run

which should run any autoformatting on your code and tell you about any errors it couldn't fix automatically. You may also install black integration into your text editor to format code automatically.

If you have already committed files before setting up the pre-commit hook with pre-commit install, you can fix everything up using pre-commit run --all-files. You need to make the fixing commit yourself after that.

Some of the hooks only run on CI by default, but you can invoke them by running with the --hook-stage manual argument.

docs.title: Releasing ipykernel
docs.text:
Releasing ipykernel is almost standard for a Python package:

  • set version for release
  • make and publish tag
  • publish release to PyPI
  • set version back to development

The one extra step for ipykernel is that we need to make separate wheels for Python 2 and 3 because the bundled kernelspec has different contents for Python 2 and 3. This affects only the 4.x branch of ipykernel as the 5+ version is only compatible Python 3.

The full release process is available below:

# make sure version is set in ipykernel/_version.py
VERSION="4.9.0"
# commit the version and make a release tag
git add ipykernel/_version.py
git commit -m "release $VERSION"
git tag -am "release $VERSION" $VERSION

# push the changes to the repo
git push
git push --tags

# publish the release to PyPI
# note the extra `python2 setup.py bdist_wheel` for creating
# the wheel for Python 2
pip install --upgrade twine
git clean -xfd
python3 setup.py sdist bdist_wheel
python2 setup.py bdist_wheel  # the extra step for the 4.x branch.
twine upload dist/*

# set the version back to '.dev' in ipykernel/_version.py
# e.g. 4.10.0.dev if we just released 4.9.0
git add ipykernel/_version.py
git commit -m "back to dev"
git push

docs.title: Execute mode
docs.text:
In [ ]: Copied! 
async def demo():
    import threading

    import anyio
    from ipywidgets import Button

    from async_kernel import Caller

    print(f"Thread name: '{threading.current_thread().name}'")
    button = Button(description="Finish")
    event = anyio.Event()
    caller = Caller()  # Use caller so the `##thread` example works.
    # This is because widget messages are received by the shell in the main thread. The event is being waited in this thread.
    button.on_click(lambda _: caller.call_no_context(event.set))
    display(button)
    await event.wait()
    button.close()
    print(f"Finished ... thread name: '{threading.current_thread().name}'")
    return "Finished"
async def demo(): import threading import anyio from ipywidgets import Button from async_kernel import Caller print(f"Thread name: '{threading.current_thread().name}'") button = Button(description="Finish") event = anyio.Event() caller = Caller() # Use caller so the `##thread` example works. # This is because widget messages are received by the shell in the main thread. The event is being waited in this thread. button.on_click(lambda _: caller.call_no_context(event.set)) display(button) await event.wait() button.close() print(f"Finished ... thread name: '{threading.current_thread().name}'") return "Finished"

Lets run it normally (queue)

docs.title: Execute mode¶
docs.text:
The user can tell the kernel that they want to execute the code concrrently in a thread or task by adding the comment ##thread or ##task respectively as the top line in the code cell.

##thread
# This code gets run in the shell via Caller.to_thread
# Only valid for this code block

Provided the frontend supports it (Jupyterlab does, VS code doesn't), multiple cells can be run at a time.

docs.title: Example¶
docs.text:
• This example requires ipywidgets
  • Ensure you are running an async kernel

Lets define a function that we'll reuse for the remainder of the notebook.

docs.title: Execute mode: task¶
docs.text:
##task
...

The task mode instructs the kernel to execute the code in a task separate to the queue, Both task and thread execute modes can be started when the kernel is busy executing. There is no imposed limitation on the number of tasks (or threads) that can be run concurrently.

See also the Caller example on how to call directly.

docs.title: Command prompt
docs.text: async-kernel (and alias async_kernel) is provided as a system executable.

docs.title: Add a kernel spec
docs.text:
Use the argument -a can be added/removed via the command line.

The argument after -a is the kernel name. Include 'trio' in the kernel name for a 'trio' backend.

Any valid kernel name is allowed do not include whitespace in the kernel name.

Add a trio kernel spec.

async-kernel -a async-trio

remove

async-kernel -r async-trio

[async_kernel.kernelspec.make_argv(kernel_name)]

docs.title: Add options
docs.text: In a

docs.title: Execute mode
docs.text: Including a comment ##thread or ##task at the start of a cell instructs the kernel to run the code asynchronously. thread and task requests are started as soon as the message is processed.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
Execute code concurrently in the main thread event loop starting without delay.

##task

docs.title: ##thread
docs.text:
Execute code concurrently in a Caller thread event loop starting without delay. The backend used will match the backend of the main event loop.

##thread
...

docs.title: ContextVars
docs.text: Execute request jobs are stored as a ContextVar which is accessible on the kernel as the property kernel.job. Using a context variable makes it possible to perform concurrent execution enabling stdio, stderr and stdin to map back to the initial job (execute request).

docs.title: Example: run a cell in a thread
docs.text:
This code will run the code in a thread.

##thread

import time

time.sleep(100)

Irrespective of the Execute mode, any code run in a cell will respect cancellation, though in this example the cancellation will only occur after the time.sleep call has returned. Should this have been run in the MainThread the time.sleep would have been cancelled immediately by means of a signal.

docs.title: Kernel variants
docs.text:
The kernel name defines the anyio backend that is used. If the name includes 'trio', a trio backed will be used (trio installation should be done separately).

There are two 'built in' kernels.

  1. async: An anyio 'asyncio' backend.
  2. async-trio: An anyio 'trio' backend (requires trio - install manually).

docs.title: Enabling / disabling kernels
docs.text: Kernels can be added/removed via the command line.

docs.title: Add
docs.text: async-kernel -add async-trio

docs.title: Remove
docs.text: async-kernel -remove async-trio
